lesson_title: Four Times the Road: The Work-Energy Theorem
hook_text: Double your speed and your brakes suddenly need FOUR times the road. Here's the equation behind it.
clip_script: Hold a twenty-five-kilogram crate of tiles against your chest, dead still, arms shaking — and physics writes down: zero work done. Zero! Because work isn't effort. Work is force times distance ALONG the force. Your push is up, the crate went nowhere — no distance, no work. Carry it down a corridor at the same height? Still zero: force up, motion sideways, and a sideways force pays nothing. Only lifting it onto the trailer makes the meter run — force up, motion up, energy delivered. Now the part that matters on the road. Every moving thing carries an energy bank account: a half m v squared. Net work is the bank statement — deposits speed you up, withdrawals slow you down. And that balance grows with the SQUARE of your speed. Sixty to one-twenty doesn't double your kinetic energy, it QUADRUPLES it — and your brakes, with the same force, must claw back four times the joules over four times the metres. Same car, same brakes, four times the road. That's not a warning sign on the highway. That's the work-energy theorem doing arithmetic.
visual_style: A trembling figure clutching a crate with a joule counter frozen at zero; the counter spinning to life as the crate rises onto a trailer; then a split screen of two identical cars braking from 60 and 120 with energy bars and skid marks stretching as squares.
mood: Playful and contrarian, hardening into road-safety punch.
pacing: Comic beat on the frozen zero, quick lift payoff, then a driving drum build into the four-times-the-road reveal.
